title: A song learns to sing in pairs
work: Nocturne in D♭ major, Op. 27 No. 2
question: How do Pachmann and Lévy make a single piano sing in two voices?
intro: The first D♭-major melody sounds like a singer alone above rippling left-hand notes. Soon the right hand adds a second voice, in thirds and sixths, and each return dresses the song more elaborately. Pachmann and Lévy each have to make two voices breathe through one hand.

recordings.label: Vladimir de Pachmann, 1925
recordings.note: Pachmann plays his own Baldwin at Hayes, with extra notes in bars 30–32.

recordings.label: Frank Lévy, c. 2014
recordings.note: Lévy’s teachers included Maria Tipo and Leon Fleisher; this nocturne comes from his Musopen Chopin project.

passages.label: Opening song
passages.note: The melody begins on F above flowing D♭-major broken chords. Long right-hand notes float over the left hand’s six-note sweeps.

passages.label: The song becomes a duet
passages.note: A second note joins the melody: the right hand sings in thirds as the bass turns towards B♭ minor.

passages.label: The first homecoming
passages.note: F returns above a low D♭. The opening song comes home, with fresh ornaments gathering round its long notes.

passages.label: The third verse
passages.note: The melody returns for the third time; its continuation will spill into a long flourish climbing and falling across the keyboard.

passages.label: D♭ holds the bass
passages.note: D♭ stays in the bass while pairs of notes descend above it, marked dolcissimo — very sweetly.
